current_episode.title: Proving the impact of air quality interventions and low emission zones with data detective Kate Barnard

guest.bio_context: Kate Barnard spent 22 years in a corporate career at Rolls-Royce before founding Enjoy the Air, an evidence-based air quality intelligence company. She describes herself as a data detective with a passion for finding solutions through data analysis. Her business partner Errol Kruger brought the air quality focus to the venture, which is now two and a half years old.

context.real_quote: The local authorities in the UK have a legal legislative requirement to document and provide evidence of their air quality and it is quite surprising how many do not meet it.
key_stats: 48% of 18 to 24-year-olds would relocate to a city with better air quality, compared to lower rates in older age groups (Yonder polling of 4,000 UK residents, commissioned by Enjoy the Air)
53% of Londoners support the clean air zone following extension with the ultra low emission zone
£42.88 million annual NHS healthcare costs attributable to air pollution (policy work cited)
Between just shy of £20 billion per year in wider economic costs when including infrastructure and investment impacts of air pollution
17% of UK public knows where to find air quality information (Enjoy the Air polling)
£9 per day charge for Bristol's low emission zone
£250,000 SEIS tax relief eligibility limit for startups (increased from £150,000 in April under the mini budget)
22 years career at Rolls-Royce before founding Enjoy the Air
2.5 years since Enjoy the Air was founded
£65,000 in de minimis grant funding received by Enjoy the Air (reducing SEIS eligibility by that amount)
April 2024: SEIS limit increased from £150,000 to £250,000
entities: North East and North Cumbria ICB

Hello and welcome to the Responsible Finance Podcast. It's a return visit for Kate Barnard, founder of Enjoy the Air, after a 22-year corporate career with Rolls-Royce. And in this episode which we recorded in May this year. Kate covers how we can model the effect of interventions on air quality, the impact of low emission zones, which local authorities are doing good work on air quality and what others can learn from them and research showing public support for low emission zones but what that actually tells us and how we can affect behaviour change. There's loads in here too about startup culture, startup finance, startup support and what corporates can do better and funders can do better to help startups survive and thrive. Kate is a self-confessed data detective and it was a pleasure to catch up with her. Let's hear from her now. Kate Barnard, founder and chief executive of evidence-based air quality intelligence company Enjoy the Air. Thank you for coming back on the podcast. How are you doing, Kate? Yes, really well, actually. Thank you, Jamie. Really delighted to speak to you again. Super. Well, so much has developed since we last had a conversation. First of all, some very interesting research that you have commissioned about the public's attitude to air quality, with a staggering number saying they would consider moving to another city for better air quality. Tell us a little bit more about that. Yes, this was a polling we commissioned through Yonder that would nominally be to about 1,000 people but actually our reach was to 4 000 people across the uk and across all areas and we can segment the data by region now and i was absolutely astounded that the younger population between 18 to 24 year olds would actually vote with their feet so 48 of them would move a location to a city or a place that has much better air quality. So that's a big contrast to people over 65 years old. It's a big contrast to the general population as well. But where are the cities where this is most pronounced? This is predominantly in London, Manchester, Birmingham and Liverpool are the bigger cities most at risk of losing their residents. The survey you mentioned by Yonder, They enjoy the air commission. It demonstrates the sort of cause and effect of air pollution, one being that cities could lose people who are their workforce now and in the future. What did you find most surprising, though, about the results? I think for me, the business is two and a half years old. And before I started this business, my passion really is being a detective around data and finding solutions. it wasn't the topic of air quality that was my business partner Errol Kruger that was his passion was on the air quality so I'd never really considered it something I should think about that there was a problem that we even measured it I guess because you can't see it so the fact that a lot of people are now starting to think about it and it's becoming on their radar are, that's been really amazing. People are definitely thinking more about what affects their health and livelihood now. Yes, absolutely. And so air quality, a threat to health, a threat to life expectancy worldwide. You mentioned you're a data detective. We understand now, I think, that air quality has an effect on asthma, coronary heart disease, diabetes, lots of other things too. You talked when I spoke with you last time about a certification that Enjoy the Air has developed. Tell us a little bit more then about the Halo certification that you have developed at Enjoy the Air, the sort of purpose of it and how it works and with whom. pending_qa.q: What level of public support exists for clean air zones in major UK cities?
pending_qa.r: Research commissioned by Enjoy the Air found that 53% of Londoners support the clean air zone following its extension with the ultra low emission zone. The research emphasizes that communicating the health benefits and what's in it for the public, beyond just funding public transport, is crucial for gaining support.

pending_qa.q: What are the annual economic costs of air pollution in the UK across health and wider economic infrastructure?
pending_qa.r: According to policy work cited by Kate Barnard, the NHS healthcare costs from air pollution are approximately 42.88 million pounds, but when looking at the wider economic infrastructure including investment and where people live, the costs rise to between just shy of 20 billion pounds per year.

pending_qa.q: How does the SEIS tax relief scheme interact with grant funding for early-stage startups?
pending_qa.r: Grant funding classified as de minimis counts directly against SEIS eligibility. Kate Barnard explains that when the SEIS limit increased from £150,000 to £250,000 in April under the mini budget, her £65,000 in grant funding reduced her SEIS eligibility to £185,000, creating a situation where funding is given with one hand and taken with the other.

pending_qa.q: What funding gaps do corporates and grant providers typically miss when supporting early-stage startups?
pending_qa.r: Kate Barnard identifies that grants do not fund sales, marketing and commercialization, yet funders want to see traction before awarding grants. She advises corporates to fund the gaps and fund things that nobody else is funding, rather than duplicating support that everyone else is already providing, and to ensure projects are funded 100% upfront rather than in arrears.

pending_qa.q: What regulatory recognition has the HALO certification achieved?
pending_qa.r: The HALO certification went through a 14-month process with the UK Intellectual Property Office to become a legally recognized trademarked certification, which also serves as proof of intellectual property for investor traction since data-based businesses cannot patent software.
